# Introduction

"Do different penguin species differ in their overall physical characteristics, and does MANOVA provide additional insight compared with conducting separate univariate ANOVAs?"

# Data

The data was collected for research that was conducted as part of the Palmer Station, Antarctica, Long-Term Ecological Research program which was supported by grants through the National Science Foundation, Office of Polar Programs (NSF-OPP). Data was originally listed as three separate datasets within the Palmer Station Long-Term Ecological Research (PAL-LTER) data system and was combined into the single Palmer penguins dataset. Data were collected and made available by Dr. Kristen Gorman and the Palmer Station, Antarctica LTER, a member of the Long Term Ecological Research Network. The data used in this analysis is provided by @penguins. All analysis was performed in @R.

First we observe the dataset in @tbl-summary.

```{r, summary}
#| label: tbl-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Summary Statistics of Key Variable Means and Sample Size by Species"

summary <- penguins %>%
  group_by(species) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_bill_length = mean(bill_length_mm),
    mean_bill_depth = mean(bill_depth_mm),
    mean_flipper_length = mean(flipper_length_mm),
    mean_body_mass = mean(body_mass_g)
  )

knitr::kable(
  summary %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~round(.x, 3))),
  caption = "Summary Statistics of Penguin Measurements",
  booktabs = TRUE
)
```

The species groups are not exactly equal in size. That is not automatically a problem, but you should report the group counts and examine the assumptions carefully


Since MANOVA does not work well with strongly positively correlated variables, I calculate the correlation matrix and present the results in @tbl-correlation From the results, we see that bill length and bill depth are weakly negatively correlated and that flipper length and body mass are strongly correlated. Since MANOVA we may expect results to be inflated

```{r, tbl-correlation, echo=FALSE}
#|tbl-cap: "Correlation Matrix of Physical Measurements"
cor_matrix <- cor(
                  penguins[, 2:5],
                  use = "complete.obs"
              )

knitr::kable(
  round(cor_matrix, 3),
  caption = "Correlation Matrix of Penguin Measurements",
  digits = 3,
  booktabs = TRUE
)
```



```{r}
penguins_long <- penguins %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(
      bill_length_mm,
      bill_depth_mm,
      flipper_length_mm,
      body_mass_g
    ),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "measurement"
  )

ggplot(penguins_long,
       aes(x = species, y = measurement, fill = species)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free_y") +

    title = "Body Measurements Across Penguin Species",
    x = "Penguin Species",

  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),

  )
```


# Methods

In order to investigate whether penguin species differ in their physical measurements I will consider four characteristics simultaneously: bill length, bill depth, flipper length, and body mass. First, I will start with four multiple univariate ANOVAs tested on each of the four characteristics. The four one-way ANOVAs will test whether penguin species differ across bill length, bill depth, flipper length, and body mass simultaneously. Each ANOVA tests whether the mean of one dependent variable differs across the three species groups. The general one-way ANOVA model is $$Y_{ij} = \mu + \alpha_i + \epsilon_{ij} $$ where $Y_{ij}$ is the observed measurement for the $j$-th penguin for each species, $i$. $\mu$ is the overall population mean. $\alpha_i$ is the effect of the $i$-th species. $\epsilon_{ij}$ is the random error associated with each observation. This error tern is assumed to be independently and normally distributed with mean zero and variance $\epsilon_{ij} \sim N(0,\sigma^2)$.



For each of the individual univariate ANOVAs, I will have a set of hypotheses for a total of four. My Null Hypothesis for each characteristic will be $$H_0: \mu_{Adelie}=\mu_{Chinstrap}=\mu_{Gentoo}$$ with an alternative hypothesis of $$ H_A: At \enspace least \enspace one \enspace species \enspace mean \enspace differs $$

 
The limitation is that each ANOVA examines one outcome independently. This means we aren't directly testing whether penguin species affects the overall combination of physical characteristics.

The general one-way MANOVA model is $$Y_{ij} = \mu + \alpha_i + \epsilon_{ij} $$ where $Y_{ij}$ is the observed measurement for the $j$-th penguin for each species, $i$. $\mu$ is the overall population mean. $\alpha_i$ is the effect of the $i$-th species. $\epsilon_{ij}$ is the random error associated with each observation. This error tern is assumed to be independently and normally distributed with mean zero and variance $\epsilon_{ij} \sim N(0,\sigma^2)$.

In addition to the three separate models, I will use MANOVA which considers all four dependent variables simultaneously.


MANOVA tests whether the three cylinder groups have significantly different multivariate mean vectors.

In other words, it asks:

Do cars with different cylinder counts differ in their overall performance profiles when fuel efficiency, horsepower, and quarter-mile time are considered together?

Since MANOVA evaluates the combined mean vectors, we have the null hypothesis which states that all three species have equal population mean vectors $$H_0:\mu_{Adelie}=\mu_{Adelie}=\mu_{Adelie}$$ and the alternative hypothesis $$ H_A: At \enspace least \enspace one \enspace mean \enspace vector \enspace differs$$

If the p-value associated with Pillai's Trace is below 0.05, you reject the null hypothesis.

This indicates that the penguin species differ significantly in their combined physical characteristics.

However, it does not identify which specific measurements differ.

MANOVA has several advantages:

It accounts for correlations between dependent variables.

It provides an overall multivariate test.

It can identify group differences that might not be apparent when looking at each outcome separately.

It avoids treating multiple related outcomes as entirely independent tests.

One particularly important point for your project: conducting three separate ANOVAs increases the overall Type I error rate unless you adjust for multiple comparisons.

MANOVA provides an overall test before you investigate individual outcomes.

# Results

```{r}
# Four univariate ANOVA
anova_bill_length <- aov(bill_length_mm ~ species, data = penguins)
anova_bill_depth <- aov(bill_depth_mm ~ species, data = penguins)
anova_flipper <- aov(flipper_length_mm ~ species, data = penguins)
anova_body <- aov(body_mass_g ~ species, data = penguins)

#summary(anova_bill_length)
#summary(anova_bill_depth)
#summary(anova_flipper)
#summary(anova_body)

anova_models <- list(
  "Bill Length" = anova_bill_length,
  "Bill Depth" = anova_bill_depth,
  "Flipper Length" = anova_flipper,
  "Body Mass" = anova_body
)

anova_table <- bind_rows(
  lapply(names(anova_models), function(variable) {

    result <- summary(anova_models[[variable]])[[1]]

    data.frame(
      Variable = variable,
      df = result[1, "Df"],
      F_statistic = result[1, "F value"],
      p_value = result[1, "Pr(>F)"]
    )
  })
) %>%
  mutate(
    F_statistic = round(F_statistic, 3),
    p_value_display = format.pval(p_value, digits = 3),
    Significance = case_when(
      p_value < 0.001 ~ "***",
      p_value < 0.01  ~ "**",
      p_value < 0.05  ~ "*",
      TRUE ~ ""
    )
  ) %>%
  select(
    Variable,
    df,
    F_statistic,
    p_value_display,
    Significance
  )

knitr::kable(
  anova_table,
  col.names = c(
    "Dependent Variable",
    "Degrees of Freedom",
    "F-statistic",
    "P-value",
    "Significance"
  ),
  caption = "One-Way ANOVA Results by Penguin Species",
  booktabs = TRUE
)
```

```{r}
# Mulitivariate MANOVA
manova_model <- manova(
  cbind(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g) ~ species,
  data = penguins
)

#summary(manova_model, test = "Pillai")

# Extract MANOVA results
manova_result <- summary(manova_model, test = "Pillai")$stats

manova_table <- data.frame(
  Test = "Pillai's Trace",
  Pillai = manova_result[1, "Pillai"],
  F_statistic = manova_result[1, "approx F"],
  df = manova_result[1, "num Df"],
  Residual_df = manova_result[1, "den Df"],
  p_value = manova_result[1, "Pr(>F)"]
) %>%
  mutate(
    across(c(Pillai, F_statistic), ~round(.x, 3)),
    p_value = format.pval(p_value, digits = 3),
    Significance = case_when(
      as.numeric(p_value) < 0.001 ~ "***",
      as.numeric(p_value) < 0.01 ~ "**",
      as.numeric(p_value) < 0.05 ~ "*",
      TRUE ~ ""
    )
  )

knitr::kable(
  manova_table,
  caption = "MANOVA Results Using Pillai's Trace",
  col.names = c(
    "Test",
    "Pillai's Trace",
    "Approx. F",
    "Numerator df",
    "Denominator df",
    "P-value",
    "Significance"
  ),
  booktabs = TRUE
)
```

```{r}
# Extract follow-up ANOVA results
manova_aov <- summary.aov(manova_model)

manova_followup <- bind_rows(
  lapply(names(manova_aov), function(variable) {

    result <- manova_aov[[variable]]

    data.frame(
      Variable = variable,
      df = result[1, "Df"],
      F_statistic = result[1, "F value"],
      p_value = result[1, "Pr(>F)"]
    )
  })
) %>%
  mutate(
    F_statistic = round(F_statistic, 3),
    p_value_display = format.pval(p_value, digits = 3),
    Significance = case_when(
      p_value < 0.001 ~ "***",
      p_value < 0.01 ~ "**",
      p_value < 0.05 ~ "*",
      TRUE ~ ""
    )
  ) %>%
  select(
    Variable,
    df,
    F_statistic,
    p_value_display,
    Significance
  )

knitr::kable(
  manova_followup,
  col.names = c(
    "Dependent Variable",
    "Degrees of Freedom",
    "F-statistic",
    "P-value",
    "Significance"
  ),
  caption = "Univariate Follow-up Tests from MANOVA",
  booktabs = TRUE
)
```


# Discussion

You should therefore discuss the assumptions of MANOVA:

Multivariate normality within groups.

Homogeneity of covariance matrices.

Independence of observations.

Absence of problematic multicollinearity.

You should also check the correlations among MPG, horsepower, and quarter-mile time.

If your dependent variables are highly correlated, this gives you an opportunity to explain why examining their relationships simultaneously is useful.

Also, be careful not to claim that MANOVA is automatically better. Its value depends on the research question, the relationship between the dependent variables, and whether its assumptions are reasonably satisfied.


This case study demonstrates the advantages of multivariate data analysis by comparing separate univariate ANOVAs with MANOVA when examining physical differences among penguin species. While individual ANOVAs provide information about differences in specific physical measurements, MANOVA evaluates whether species differ across multiple characteristics simultaneously while accounting for relationships among the dependent variables. This provides a more comprehensive understanding of group differences and reduces the need to rely exclusively on multiple independent hypothesis tests. Therefore, multivariate analysis is particularly valuable when research questions involve several related outcome variables.
